claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed jointly by intrinsic lattice distortion and controlled surface oxidation.
Intrinsic lattice distortion retards atomic diffusion in the nanoparticle core.
Retarded core diffusion limits phase segregation and coarsening.
Low oxygen partial pressure produces a thin, self-passivating surface oxide layer.
The passivating oxide shell suppresses surface-atom mobility and sintering.
Core lattice distortion and surface passivation act synergistically to preserve structural integrity and chemical uniformity at high temperatures.
The starting nanoparticles have an initially uniform elemental distribution.
The starting nanoparticles have high lattice strain.
Low-oxygen treatment will yield a stable core-shell structure.
Low-oxygen-treated nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than inert-treated nanoparticles.
Low-oxygen-treated nanoparticles will exhibit less sintering than inert-treated nanoparticles.
Inert-treated nanoparticles will undergo significant diffusion-driven phase separation and coarsening because they lack surface passivation.
Low-oxygen-treated nanoparticles will maintain more consistent catalytic activity over repeated cycles than inert-treated nanoparticles.
Low-oxygen-treated nanoparticles will show less degradation of electrical and thermal properties than inert-treated nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to near-equiatomic nanoparticles in the 5–20 nm size range.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to larger particles or substantially different compositions.
Excessively high oxygen levels can cause detrimental oxidation and invalidate the beneficial-passivation regime.
Lattice distortion is a recognized kinetic barrier to diffusion.
